skills.name: Skim Reading
skills.description: Learner reads headings and first sentence of each paragraph only, then produces a correct general topic statement. Simulated skim: platform reveals only [HEADING] lines and first sentence of each [PARA] block.
skills.deliveryMode: TEXT — Learner types topic statement. Latency measured from text display to submission.
skills.questionFormat: Open response — one sentence stating what the whole text is about
skills.defaultPrompt: Skim the headings and first sentences only. What is the whole text about? Answer in one sentence.

tolerance.condition: Topic statement covers >=0.60 of text content (GREEN), even with simple phrasing.
Coverage 0.40–0.60 (AMBER). Log; count as pass if latency also passes.
Coverage <0.40 — statement covers only one section.
Learner reproduces the opening sentence of the text verbatim (copying >=60%).
Latency >140 sec — learner read the full text, not just headings/first sentences.

recovery.action: Timed reveal: headings and first sentences shown one at a time on click. Timer enforced on next attempt.
Prompt: 'What is the whole text about, not just one part?'
System prompts: 'In your own words, what is the whole text about?'

items.title: The Water Cycle
items.passage: [HEADING] The Water Cycle [First sentence] Water moves continuously between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere in a process called the water cycle. [SUBHEADING] Evaporation and Condensation [First sentence] When the sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes, it turns into water vapour and rises into the air. [SUBHEADING] Precipitation and Collection [First sentence] When clouds hold enough water droplets, the water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail — this is called precipitation.

answerKey.reference: Water moves between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere in a continuous process called the water cycle.

items.title: How Solar Energy Works
items.passage: [HEADING] How Solar Energy Works [First sentence] Solar energy is electricity produced from sunlight, and it is one of the fastest-growing energy sources in the world. [SUBHEADING] Capturing Sunlight [First sentence] Solar panels are made of cells that absorb sunlight and convert it directly into electricity. [SUBHEADING] Benefits and Limitations [First sentence] Solar energy produces no pollution when generating electricity, which helps reduce climate change.

answerKey.reference: Solar energy converts sunlight into electricity and is growing as a clean, renewable energy source.

items.title: Animal Migration
items.passage: [HEADING] Animal Migration [First sentence] Migration is the seasonal movement of animals from one place to another, usually to find food, warmth, or safe breeding grounds. [SUBHEADING] Why Animals Migrate [First sentence] Most animals migrate because their food supply changes with the seasons. [SUBHEADING] How Animals Navigate [First sentence] Scientists have discovered that many animals use the Earth's magnetic field like a compass to navigate.

answerKey.reference: Many animals migrate seasonally to find food or breeding grounds, using remarkable navigation abilities.

items.title: The Amazon Rainforest
items.passage: [HEADING] The Amazon Rainforest [First sentence] The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, covering more than five million square kilometres across nine countries in South America. [SUBHEADING] Biodiversity [First sentence] Scientists estimate that the Amazon contains around 10% of all species on Earth. [SUBHEADING] Threats and Importance [First sentence] The Amazon is often called 'the lungs of the Earth' because its trees absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

answerKey.reference: The Amazon Rainforest is the world's largest rainforest and a vital resource for global biodiversity and climate.

items.title: How Vaccines Work
items.passage: [HEADING] How Vaccines Work [First sentence] Vaccines teach the body's immune system to recognise and fight specific diseases without the person having to get sick first. [SUBHEADING] The Immune Response [First sentence] When a vaccine is given, it introduces a weakened or inactive form of a disease-causing germ — or just a small piece of it — into the body. [SUBHEADING] Community Protection [First sentence] When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily — even people who cannot be vaccinated (such as very young babies) are protected.

answerKey.reference: Vaccines protect individuals and communities from disease by training the immune system to fight specific germs.

items.title: The History of Writing
items.passage: [HEADING] The History of Writing [First sentence] Writing is one of humanity's most important inventions, allowing people to store and share information across time and distance. [SUBHEADING] Early Writing Systems [First sentence] The oldest known writing system is cuneiform, developed by the Sumerians of ancient Mesopotamia around 3 400 BCE. [SUBHEADING] Alphabets and Modern Writing [First sentence] The first true alphabet — in which each symbol represents a sound — appeared around 2 000 BCE in the region that is now the Middle East.

answerKey.reference: Writing is a vital human invention that began thousands of years ago and has evolved into the systems we use today.

items.title: Why Recycling Matters
items.passage: [HEADING] Why Recycling Matters [First sentence] Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new products, reducing the need to extract and use raw natural resources. [SUBHEADING] Reducing Landfill Waste [First sentence] Without recycling, most household waste goes to landfill sites where it breaks down slowly, releasing harmful gases. [SUBHEADING] Saving Energy and Resources [First sentence] Making products from recycled materials uses far less energy than starting from raw materials.

answerKey.reference: Recycling reduces waste and saves energy and natural resources by reprocessing used materials into new products.

items.title: Coral Reefs in Danger
items.passage: [HEADING] Coral Reefs in Danger [First sentence] Coral reefs are underwater ecosystems built by tiny animals called coral polyps, and they support more species of marine life than any other ocean habitat. [SUBHEADING] What Threatens Coral Reefs [First sentence] Rising ocean temperatures caused by climate change trigger a process called coral bleaching, in which corals expel the algae living in their tissue and turn white. [SUBHEADING] Why Reefs Matter [First sentence] Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but are home to about 25% of all marine species.

answerKey.reference: Coral reefs are vital ocean ecosystems that are under serious threat from climate change and ocean acidification.

items.title: The Busy World of Honeybees
items.passage: [HEADING] The Busy World of Honeybees [First sentence] Honeybees live together in large colonies and work as a team to collect food and care for their young. [SUBHEADING] Life Inside the Hive [First sentence] Each hive has one queen, thousands of female worker bees, and male bees called drones, and every bee has its own job. [SUBHEADING] Why Bees Matter to Us [First sentence] As bees move from flower to flower they spread pollen, which helps plants make the fruits and seeds that people and animals eat.

answerKey.reference: Honeybees live and work together in colonies, and they matter to us because they pollinate the plants we rely on for food.

items.title: Climbing the World's Highest Mountain
items.passage: [HEADING] Climbing the World's Highest Mountain [First sentence] Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is the highest mountain on Earth at about 8 849 metres above sea level. [SUBHEADING] Dangers on the Mountain [First sentence] Climbers face freezing temperatures, thin air with little oxygen, and sudden storms near the summit. [SUBHEADING] The People Who Help [First sentence] Local Sherpa guides carry equipment and lead climbers, using their deep knowledge of the mountain to keep expeditions safe.

answerKey.reference: Mount Everest is the world's highest and most dangerous mountain to climb, and Sherpa guides help climbers reach the top safely.

items.title: The Amazon Rainforest
items.passage: [HEADING] The Amazon Rainforest [First sentence] The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth, stretching across nine countries in South America. [SUBHEADING] A Home for Wildlife [First sentence] Millions of species of insects, plants, birds, and mammals live in the Amazon, many found nowhere else in the world. [SUBHEADING] The Forest Under Threat [First sentence] Large areas of the rainforest are cut down each year for farming and timber, which harms wildlife and adds to climate change.

answerKey.reference: The Amazon is the world's largest rainforest and home to a huge variety of wildlife, but it is under threat from deforestation.

items.title: Why We Recycle
items.passage: [HEADING] Why We Recycle [First sentence] Recycling means turning used materials like paper, glass, and plastic into new products instead of throwing them away. [SUBHEADING] How Recycling Works [First sentence] Used materials are collected, sorted, cleaned, and then broken down so they can be made into something new. [SUBHEADING] The Benefits for the Planet [First sentence] Recycling saves natural resources, uses less energy, and reduces the rubbish sent to landfill sites.

answerKey.reference: Recycling turns used materials into new products, which saves resources and energy and reduces waste.

items.title: The Human Heart
items.passage: [HEADING] The Human Heart [First sentence] The heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist that pumps blood around your body every second of your life. [SUBHEADING] How the Heart Works [First sentence] The heart has four chambers that squeeze in a steady rhythm to push blood through a network of blood vessels. [SUBHEADING] Keeping Your Heart Healthy [First sentence] Regular exercise, a balanced diet, and avoiding smoking all help keep the heart strong and working well.

answerKey.reference: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body, and healthy habits like exercise and good food keep it strong.

items.title: Volcanoes
items.passage: [HEADING] Volcanoes [First sentence] A volcano is an opening in the Earth's surface through which melted rock, ash, and gases can escape from deep underground. [SUBHEADING] What Causes an Eruption [First sentence] Pressure builds up beneath the surface until molten rock called magma is forced upwards and bursts out as lava. [SUBHEADING] Living Near Volcanoes [First sentence] Although eruptions can be dangerous, many people live near volcanoes because the soil around them is very fertile for farming.

answerKey.reference: Volcanoes let molten rock and gas escape from inside the Earth, and although they can be dangerous, people live near them for the fertile soil.

items.title: The History of the Bicycle
items.passage: [HEADING] The History of the Bicycle [First sentence] The bicycle has changed a great deal since the first wooden version was invented in the early 1800s. [SUBHEADING] Early Designs [First sentence] The earliest bicycles had no pedals and were pushed along the ground with the rider's feet. [SUBHEADING] The Modern Bicycle [First sentence] Today's bicycles have chains, gears, and air-filled tyres that make them faster, safer, and more comfortable to ride.

answerKey.reference: The bicycle has developed from a simple pedal-less wooden machine in the 1800s into the fast, comfortable bicycle we use today.

skills.name: Scan Reading
skills.description: Learner scans a text for a specific named detail — a date, name, or statistic — as quickly as possible, without reading the full text.
skills.deliveryMode: TEXT — Learner types the specific detail. Latency measured.
skills.questionFormat: Short answer — the specific detail only (e.g. a year, a name, a number with units)
skills.defaultPrompt: Scan the text to find the answer. Type only the specific detail.

tolerance.condition: Exact match with the target detail (name, date, number with correct units).
Minor spelling variation on a name — if unambiguously the correct person/place.
Number given without units if the number is uniquely correct (e.g. '1981' for '1981').
Wrong value, name, or date retrieved for the scan target. Even if the right type (e.g. wrong year).
Learner lists all instances of the target type rather than the specific requested detail.
Response latency >100 sec — learner is reading rather than scanning.

recovery.action: 'Look for the key word in the question, then find it on the page.' Timer enforced on next attempt.
'Which part of the text answers this question exactly? Find that sentence.'
'Which one answers the question exactly? Give only that one.'

items.passage: The Great Barrier Reef stretches for 2 300 kilometres along the northeast coast of Australia. It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981. The reef is made up of about 2 900 individual reefs and 900 islands. Every year, approximately 2 million tourists visit the area, contributing around 6.4 billion dollars to the Australian economy. Marine biologist Dr Sylvia Earle described it as 'the most spectacular marine environment on Earth.'
items.question: In what year was the Great Barrier Reef listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?

items.passage: The International Space Station (ISS) orbits Earth at an average altitude of 408 kilometres. It travels at approximately 28 000 kilometres per hour, completing one orbit every 90 minutes. The station was first launched in November 1998 and has been continuously inhabited since November 2000. Commander Chris Hadfield became famous for posting photographs and videos from the ISS. The station is jointly operated by the space agencies of the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada.
items.question: What is the average altitude at which the ISS orbits Earth?

answerKey.reference: 408 kilometres

items.passage: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when he noticed that a mould called Penicillium notatum was killing bacteria in one of his laboratory dishes. However, it was scientists Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain who developed penicillin into a usable medicine. By 1945, penicillin was being manufactured on a large scale. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945. Penicillin is still one of the most widely used antibiotics in the world today.
items.question: Who discovered penicillin?

answerKey.reference: Alexander Fleming

items.passage: Mount Everest, located on the border of Nepal and Tibet, is the highest mountain on Earth, measuring 8 849 metres above sea level. The first confirmed ascent was made on 29 May 1953 by Tenzing Norgay and Sir Edmund Hillary. Since then, more than 6 000 people have reached the summit. Each year around 800 climbers attempt the ascent. The mountain is named after Sir George Everest, the British surveyor who mapped the Indian subcontinent in the 19th century.
items.question: What is the height of Mount Everest above sea level?

answerKey.reference: 8 849 metres

items.passage: The Rosetta Stone was discovered in 1799 by French soldiers during Napoleon Bonaparte's campaign in Egypt. It is a stone slab inscribed with the same text written in three scripts: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics, Demotic script, and ancient Greek. Scholar Jean-François Champollion finally decoded the hieroglyphics in 1822, using the Greek text as a guide. The stone is currently on display at the British Museum in London, where it has been since 1802. It is one of the most visited objects in the museum.
items.question: In what year was the Rosetta Stone discovered?

items.passage: The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons — nerve cells that send and receive signals throughout the body. The brain makes up only about 2% of body weight but uses around 20% of the body's total energy. Neuroscientist Dr Antonio Damasio has studied how emotions influence decision-making in the brain. The cerebral cortex, the outer layer of the brain, is responsible for thinking, language, and memory. The brain continues developing until around age 25 in humans.
items.question: Approximately how many neurons does the human brain contain?

answerKey.reference: 86 billion neurons

items.passage: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the world's longest railway line, stretching 9 289 kilometres from Moscow in Russia to Vladivostok on the Pacific coast. Construction began in 1891 under Tsar Alexander III and was completed in 1916. The full journey takes approximately six days by train and passes through eight time zones. Engineer Gennady Fadeev oversaw a major modernisation of the railway in the early 2000s. Approximately 30% of Russia's freight is transported along this route.
items.question: How long is the Trans-Siberian Railway?

answerKey.reference: 9 289 kilometres

items.passage: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867. She moved to Paris to study at the Sorbonne University, where she became the first woman to earn a doctorate in physics in France. In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. In 1911 she was awarded a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry — making her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her research on radioactivity changed the course of modern science.
items.question: In what year did Marie Curie win her second Nobel Prize?

items.passage: The Sahara Desert is the world's largest hot desert, covering approximately 9 million square kilometres across 11 African countries. Despite its reputation for sand dunes, around 70% of the Sahara is actually covered by gravel plains and rocky plateaus. Temperatures can exceed 50 degrees Celsius during the day and drop below freezing at night. Explorer René Caillié was the first European to return alive from Timbuktu in 1828. The Sahara has been expanding southward at a rate of about 48 kilometres per year.
items.question: Across how many African countries does the Sahara Desert stretch?

answerKey.reference: 11 African countries

items.passage: The printing press was invented by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440 in the German city of Mainz. Before this invention, books had to be copied by hand, which meant they were rare and expensive. Gutenberg's press could produce around 3 600 pages per day, compared to a single page per day by hand. By 1500, printing presses had produced over 20 million books across Europe. Historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that the printing press was the single most important factor in the spread of the Renaissance and the Reformation.
items.question: Who invented the printing press?

answerKey.reference: Johannes Gutenberg

items.passage: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous structures in the world. It was built over many centuries by different Chinese dynasties to protect the country from invaders. The full length of all its sections is about 21 000 kilometres. Construction began more than 2 000 years ago, and millions of workers were involved over time.
items.question: How long is the Great Wall of China in total?

answerKey.reference: About 21 000 kilometres

items.passage: Nelson Mandela was one of South Africa's most respected leaders. He spent 27 years in prison for opposing the unjust system of apartheid. After his release in 1990, he worked to bring peace to the country. In 1994, he became South Africa's first democratically elected president.
items.question: In which year did Nelson Mandela become president of South Africa?

items.passage: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. It is about 150 million kilometres away from Earth. Light from the Sun takes around eight minutes to reach us. The Sun is so large that more than one million Earths could fit inside it.
items.question: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?

answerKey.reference: About eight minutes

items.passage: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth. It can reach speeds of up to 110 kilometres per hour in short bursts while chasing prey. However, it can keep up this speed for only about 30 seconds before it needs to rest. Cheetahs live mainly in the grasslands of Africa.
items.question: What is the cheetah's top speed?

answerKey.reference: Up to 110 kilometres per hour

items.passage: The modern Olympic Games were first held in Athens, Greece, in 1896. The Games take place every four years and bring together athletes from around the world. The five rings on the Olympic flag represent the five continents that take part.
items.question: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held?

answerKey.reference: Athens

skills.name: Text Purpose Identification
skills.description: Learner identifies the primary purpose of a text — INFORM, PERSUADE, or ENTERTAIN — and gives one text-based reason naming a specific language feature.
skills.deliveryMode: TEXT or VOICE — Purpose label + one reason sentence
skills.questionFormat: Two-part response: (1) purpose label; (2) one sentence naming a specific text feature as evidence
skills.defaultPrompt: What is the main purpose of this text — INFORM, PERSUADE, or ENTERTAIN? Give one sentence naming a specific language feature in the text as your reason.

tolerance.condition: Purpose label — correct label (INFORM / PERSUADE / ENTERTAIN), exact label required.
Reason names any specific language feature from the key feature list (e.g. 'uses the word should', 'uses a statistic', 'uses humour').
Reason — paraphrase of feature acceptable if the feature type is identifiable.
Incorrect classification label.
Correct label but no textual feature given as evidence.
Reason does not reference a specific text feature (e.g. 'it uses good words').

recovery.action: Purpose feature chart: 3 features per type listed. Learner checks text against chart before answering.
'Name one specific word or feature in the text that shows this is its purpose.'
'Which specific word or phrase tells you that?'

items.passage: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food using sunlight. Inside plant cells are structures called chloroplasts, which contain a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs energy from sunlight and uses it to convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen. The plant uses the glucose for energy and growth, while the oxygen is released into the air. This process makes plants the foundation of nearly all food chains on Earth.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses factual language, scientific terms (chlorophyll, glucose), and explains a process without expressing an opinion.

items.passage: Black holes are regions of space where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape. They form when a massive star collapses at the end of its life, compressing all its mass into an extremely small, dense point called a singularity. The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape is called the event horizon. Scientists can detect black holes by observing how their gravity affects nearby stars and gas. In 2019, the first direct image of a black hole was captured by a network of radio telescopes.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses factual language, defines scientific terms, presents verified information without personal opinion.

items.passage: The global population reached 8 billion people in November 2022. It took just 12 years to add the last billion, compared to 123 years to grow from 1 billion to 2 billion in the early 1900s. Most of the current growth is happening in countries in Africa and Asia. Populations in many European countries, by contrast, are ageing and in some cases declining. Demographers project that global population will peak at around 10.4 billion people in the 2080s before levelling off.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses statistics, precise dates, and projects future data. No opinion or persuasive language.

items.passage: Earthquakes occur when energy stored in underground rocks is suddenly released, sending vibrations called seismic waves through the Earth. Most earthquakes happen along fault lines — cracks in the Earth's crust where tectonic plates meet or slide past each other. The point inside the Earth where an earthquake begins is called the focus, and the point directly above it on the surface is called the epicentre. Scientists use an instrument called a seismograph to measure the strength and location of earthquakes.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Defines terms (focus, epicentre, seismograph), explains a natural process factually.

items.passage: Every school in the country should provide free, healthy meals to all students, regardless of their family's income. Hungry children cannot concentrate in class, and study after study has shown that students who eat well perform better academically. It is simply not fair that some children arrive at school without breakfast and struggle to focus while others do not. Investing in school meals is not a cost — it is an investment in our children's futures. We must act now before another generation is left behind.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as PERSUADE (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses opinion phrases (should, must), emotive language (not fair, left behind), and a direct call to action.

items.passage: Single-use plastic bags must be banned immediately. These bags take over 500 years to decompose, and millions of them end up in our oceans every year, killing marine life and polluting beaches. The good news is that reusable bags are cheap, durable, and just as convenient. Several countries have already introduced plastic bag bans and seen significant reductions in plastic pollution within months. There is no excuse for inaction. Every bag we eliminate is a step toward a cleaner, healthier planet for everyone.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as PERSUADE (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses must, calls for immediate action, uses emotive appeal (killing marine life), positive framing of alternatives.

items.passage: Students should have a say in what topics they study at school. When learners have some choice over their education, they are more motivated, more engaged, and more likely to develop a genuine love of learning. The current system treats students as empty containers to be filled with information rather than as thinking individuals with real interests and ideas. It is time for schools to trust their students and create a more flexible curriculum. Student voice is not a luxury — it is a necessity for education that truly works.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as PERSUADE (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses should, rhetorical comparison (containers), opinion signals (it is time), emotional appeal.

items.passage: The morning my uncle tried to make pancakes for the whole family, our kitchen looked like a disaster zone within minutes. Flour covered every surface. An egg had somehow reached the ceiling. The dog was enthusiastically licking batter off the floor tiles while my aunt stood in the doorway, arms crossed, watching with an expression that suggested she was reconsidering several life decisions. The pancakes, when they finally emerged, were perfectly shaped — perfectly shaped like small, blackened biscuits. My uncle called them 'rustic.' We called them inedible. We ended up eating cereal.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as ENTERTAIN (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses humour, vivid imagery, storytelling voice, descriptive language, and comic detail.

items.passage: Nobody had warned Zara that the school's new robot assistant had a bug in its politeness settings. Every time a teacher asked it a question, it would answer correctly — then bow deeply and recite a poem. 'What is the capital of France?' asked Mr Khumalo. 'Paris,' said the robot. Then it bowed, and said: 'Roses are red, violets are blue, geography is wonderful, and so are you.' The class erupted. Mr Khumalo tried, and failed, to keep a straight face. By the end of the day, students were inventing increasingly obscure questions just to hear what poem the robot would produce.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as ENTERTAIN (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses narrative, dialogue, comic scenario, playful tone, character reactions for humour.

items.passage: The cat had decided, definitively and without consultation, that the keyboard was the best possible place to sit. This was inconvenient, as Priya was in the middle of writing an important email. She lifted the cat. The cat returned. She moved the cat to a cushion specially purchased for this purpose. The cat examined the cushion, determined it was inferior, and returned to the keyboard. The email, when finally sent, contained the phrase 'best regardsxxxxxppppppp', which Priya did not notice until after pressing send. The recipient, assuming it was a new form of greeting, replied: 'Best xxxxxppppppp to you too.'

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as ENTERTAIN (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses comic narrative, character contrast (determined cat, frustrated human), escalating absurdity, satisfying punchline.

items.passage: Our school produces bags and bags of waste every single day, and most of it could be recycled. By placing recycling bins in every classroom, we could cut our waste in half and teach everyone good habits at the same time. It is a simple change that costs almost nothing. If we truly care about our planet, we cannot keep ignoring this problem. Let's make our school a recycling school — starting today.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as PERSUADE (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).

Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses strong opinion language ('we cannot keep ignoring'), a direct call to action ('Let's make our school...'), and an emotional appeal to caring about the planet.

items.passage: Rain forms through a process that begins when the sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes. The warm water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour and rises into the sky. As the vapour cools high in the air, it turns back into tiny droplets that join to form clouds. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall to the ground as rain. This continuous movement of water is called the water cycle.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Explains a process step by step using factual language and scientific terms (water vapour, water cycle) without giving an opinion.

items.passage: Biscuit the dog had one rule in life: every shoe in the house belonged to him. It did not matter whose foot it fitted. The moment a shoe was left unguarded, Biscuit would carry it proudly to his secret pile behind the sofa. One morning, Dad hopped around the kitchen wearing one shoe and one slipper, muttering about 'that thieving hound', while Biscuit watched calmly from the doorway, looking deeply innocent and just a little pleased with himself.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as ENTERTAIN (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Tells an amusing story with a mischievous animal character, funny details (one shoe and one slipper), and a humorous ending.

items.passage: Penguins are flightless birds that live mostly in the southern half of the world. Although they cannot fly, they are excellent swimmers and use their wings like flippers to move quickly through the water. Penguins have a thick layer of fat and tightly packed feathers that keep them warm in freezing conditions. They feed on fish, squid, and small sea creatures called krill.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as INFORM (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Gives factual information about penguins' features and behaviour using a neutral, explaining tone.

items.passage: Reading is one of the best things you can do for yourself, yet too many of us spend hours scrolling on screens instead. A good book can take you to another world, teach you something new, and improve your writing without you even noticing. Just twenty minutes a day can make a real difference. Put down your phone, pick up a book, and discover what you have been missing.

checks.description: Correctly identifies the purpose as PERSUADE (choices: INFORM, PERSUADE, ENTERTAIN).
Gives a valid text-based reason. Model reason: Uses persuasive techniques: a strong opinion, direct address to the reader, and a clear call to action ('Put down your phone, pick up a book').

items.title: Volcanoes
items.passage: [HEADING] Volcanoes: Fire from the Earth [PARA] Volcanoes are openings in the Earth's crust through which magma, gases, and ash escape. They can form mountains, islands, and fertile plains. [SUBHEADING] Types of Eruption [PARA] Some volcanoes erupt violently, sending [BOLD]pyroclastic flows[/BOLD] — fast-moving rivers of hot gas and rock — down their slopes. Others release lava slowly over long periods. [SIDEBAR] The 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens in the USA removed the top 400 metres of the mountain and caused the largest landslide in recorded history. [PARA] Scientists who study volcanoes are called volcanologists. They monitor underground activity to try to predict eruptions before they happen.

items.title: Rainwater Harvesting
items.passage: [HEADING] Collecting Rainwater at Home [PARA] Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rain that falls on rooftops and other surfaces for later use. It reduces household water bills and conserves municipal water supplies. [SUBHEADING] How It Works [PARA] Gutters channel rainwater from the roof into a storage tank or barrel. A [BOLD]first-flush diverter[/BOLD] removes the initial dirty water before clean rain enters the tank. [CAPTION] A rooftop collection system can store up to 5 000 litres of rainwater per heavy rainfall event. [PARA] Collected rainwater can be used to water gardens, wash cars, or flush toilets. In some systems it is filtered and purified for drinking.

items.title: Deep Sea Creatures
items.passage: [HEADING] Life in the Deep Ocean [PARA] The deep ocean — below 200 metres — is one of the least explored places on Earth. It is completely dark, very cold, and under enormous pressure. [SUBHEADING] Bioluminescence [PARA] Many deep sea animals produce their own light through a process called [BOLD]bioluminescence[/BOLD]. This light is used to attract prey, communicate, or confuse predators. [SUBHEADING] Food Sources [PARA] Without sunlight, deep sea creatures cannot rely on plants for food. Many feed on [BOLD]marine snow[/BOLD] — tiny particles of dead material that drift down from shallower water. [SIDEBAR] The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure from its head to attract prey in the darkness.

items.title: The Heart
items.passage: [HEADING] The Human Heart [PARA] The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body. An adult heart beats approximately 100 000 times a day. [SUBHEADING] The Four Chambers [PARA] The heart is divided into four chambers: two [BOLD]atria[/BOLD] (upper chambers) and two [BOLD]ventricles[/BOLD] (lower chambers). The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. [CAPTION] The left ventricle has thicker walls than the right because it must pump blood to the whole body. [SIDEBAR] During exercise, the heart can beat up to 200 times per minute in a trained athlete.

items.title: Ancient Rome
items.passage: [HEADING] The Rise and Fall of Ancient Rome [PARA] Ancient Rome grew from a small city on the banks of the Tiber River into one of the greatest empires the world has ever seen. [SUBHEADING] The Roman Republic [PARA] For centuries, Rome was governed as a republic — citizens voted for leaders called [BOLD]consuls[/BOLD] who shared power to prevent any one person from becoming too powerful. [SUBHEADING] The Roman Empire [PARA] In 27 BCE, Augustus became the first Roman [BOLD]emperor[/BOLD], ending the republic and beginning an era of imperial rule that lasted for centuries. [CAPTION] At its height, the Roman Empire controlled territories across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East.

items.title: Urban Farming
items.passage: [HEADING] Growing Food in the City [PARA] Urban farming is the practice of growing food within cities, on rooftops, in community gardens, or in indoor vertical farms. It is growing rapidly as cities look for ways to produce fresh food locally. [SUBHEADING] Vertical Farming [PARA] In vertical farms, crops grow in stacked layers under [BOLD]LED lighting[/BOLD] with no soil — only nutrient-rich water. This method uses 95% less water than traditional farming. [SIDEBAR] Singapore produces 10% of its leafy vegetables through urban farming despite having very little agricultural land. [SUBHEADING] Community Gardens [PARA] Community gardens allow city residents to grow vegetables and fruit in shared spaces, improving access to fresh food and creating green spaces in built-up areas.

items.title: Renewable Energy
items.passage: [HEADING] Power from Nature [PARA] Renewable energy comes from sources that never run out, such as sunlight, wind, and moving water, and countries are turning to it to reduce pollution. [SUBHEADING] Solar Power [PARA] Solar panels capture energy from the sun and turn it into [BOLD]electricity[/BOLD] that can power homes and schools. [SIDEBAR] In 2022, renewable sources produced almost 30% of the world's electricity. [SUBHEADING] Wind Power [PARA] Tall wind turbines use the force of the wind to spin blades that generate power, even in remote areas.

items.title: Sharks
items.passage: [HEADING] Sharks: Rulers of the Ocean [PARA] Sharks have lived in the world's oceans for more than 400 million years, long before the dinosaurs. [SUBHEADING] Built to Hunt [PARA] A shark's body is streamlined for speed, and its rows of sharp [BOLD]teeth[/BOLD] are replaced throughout its life. [SIDEBAR] Most of the 500 shark species are harmless to humans, and attacks are extremely rare. [SUBHEADING] Sharks in Danger [PARA] Millions of sharks are caught each year, and several species are now at risk of disappearing.

items.passage: [HEADING] Life in Ancient Egypt [PARA] The ancient Egyptians built one of the longest-lasting civilisations in history along the River Nile. [SUBHEADING] The Importance of the Nile [PARA] Each year the Nile flooded and left behind rich [BOLD]silt[/BOLD] that made the soil perfect for farming. [SUBHEADING] Pyramids and Pharaohs [PARA] Kings called pharaohs ruled Egypt, and huge stone pyramids were built as their tombs. [SIDEBAR] The Great Pyramid of Giza took around 20 years to build.

items.title: Healthy Eating

[SUBHEADING] A Balanced Diet [PARA] A balanced diet includes fruit, vegetables, grains, and protein, with only small amounts of [BOLD]sugar[/BOLD]. [SIDEBAR] Health experts recommend at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day. [SUBHEADING] Drinking Water [PARA] Water keeps the body working properly, and children should drink it regularly throughout the day.

[SUBHEADING] How It Works [PARA] Information travels as tiny pieces of [BOLD]data[/BOLD] that move between devices in fractions of a second. [SUBHEADING] Staying Safe Online [PARA] Users should protect their passwords and be careful about what they share. [SIDEBAR] More than five billion people now use the internet worldwide.

items.title: Earthquakes
items.passage: [HEADING] When the Ground Shakes [PARA] An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement deep inside the Earth. [SUBHEADING] What Causes Earthquakes [PARA] The Earth's outer layer is cracked into huge pieces called [BOLD]tectonic plates[/BOLD] that slowly move and sometimes slip. [SIDEBAR] Scientists use a tool called a seismometer to measure how strong an earthquake is. [SUBHEADING] Staying Safe [PARA] During an earthquake, people are advised to take cover under sturdy furniture and stay away from windows.

items.title: Migratory Birds
items.passage: [HEADING] The Great Journeys of Birds [PARA] Many birds travel thousands of kilometres each year in a journey called migration. [SUBHEADING] Why Birds Migrate [PARA] Birds migrate to find food and warmer weather when the [BOLD]seasons[/BOLD] change. [SUBHEADING] Finding the Way [PARA] Birds use the sun, the stars, and the Earth's magnetic field to navigate. [SIDEBAR] The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying from pole to pole each year.

items.title: Deserts of the World

[SUBHEADING] A Harsh Climate [PARA] Deserts can be scorching by day and freezing by night because there are few clouds to trap [BOLD]heat[/BOLD]. [SIDEBAR] The Sahara in Africa is the largest hot desert in the world. [SUBHEADING] Surviving the Desert [PARA] Desert plants and animals have special features, such as storing water, that help them survive with very little moisture.

skills.description: Learner reads a structured data text presenting two or more comparable entities and answers a comparison or inference question by extracting >=2 data points and producing a comparison statement.
skills.deliveryMode: TEXT — Learner writes a comparison or inference statement
skills.questionFormat: Open response — comparison statement referencing >=2 data points with comparison language
skills.defaultPrompt: Read the data, then answer the question. Use at least two data points from the text and comparison language (e.g. more than, less than, while, compared to).

tolerance.condition: >=2 data points from the structured data text; comparison language present; directional accuracy correct.
Comparison language — 'more than', 'less than', 'both', 'while', 'compared to', 'whereas', 'higher', 'lower', 'greater', 'fewer' — any of these qualify.
Only one data point mentioned. Comparison requires >=2.
Data points described in separate sentences without comparative framing.
Comparison direction inverted (e.g. 'A is greater than B' when data shows B > A).

recovery.action: 'Your answer must reference at least two values from the data. Add the second.'
Sentence frame: '___ is [more/less] than ___ because the data shows ___.'

items.dataText: DATA: Annual rainfall (millimetres) in three cities: Cape Town: 515 mm Johannesburg: 713 mm Durban: 1 009 mm Data source: South African Weather Service, 2023.
items.question: Which city receives the most rainfall per year, and how much more does it receive than Cape Town?

answerKey.reference: Durban receives the most rainfall (1 009 mm). It receives 494 mm more than Cape Town (515 mm).

items.dataText: DATA: Average daily screen time for learners in three age groups (hours): Ages 10–12: 4.2 hours Ages 13–15: 6.5 hours Ages 16–18: 7.8 hours Source: Digital Health Survey, 2023.
items.question: How does screen time change as learners get older? Use at least two data points in your answer.

answerKey.reference: Screen time increases with age. Learners aged 10–12 average 4.2 hours, while those aged 16–18 average 7.8 hours — an increase of 3.6 hours per day.

items.dataText: DATA: Plastic waste generated per person per year (kilograms): United States: 130 kg United Kingdom: 99 kg South Africa: 38 kg India: 4 kg Source: OECD Global Plastics Report, 2022.
items.question: Which country generates the least plastic waste per person, and how does it compare to the highest?

answerKey.reference: India generates the least plastic waste per person (4 kg). The United States generates the most (130 kg) — more than 32 times more than India.

items.dataText: DATA: Number of books read per year by learners in three schools: School A: 14 books per learner School B: 8 books per learner School C: 22 books per learner All schools are in the same city. School C has a dedicated reading period each day.
items.question: What does the data suggest about the effect of a dedicated reading period on the number of books read?

answerKey.reference: School C, which has a dedicated reading period, has learners who read 22 books per year — the highest of the three schools. This suggests that a dedicated reading period may increase the number of books learners read.

items.dataText: DATA: Water usage per household per day (litres) in three towns: Town X (water restrictions in place): 180 litres Town Y (no restrictions): 320 litres Town Z (no restrictions): 295 litres Source: Municipal water authority report, 2023.
items.question: Compare the water usage of Town X to Towns Y and Z. What does the data suggest about water restrictions?

answerKey.reference: Town X uses 180 litres per day, while Town Y uses 320 litres and Town Z uses 295 litres. Town X uses significantly less water than the other two towns. The data suggests that water restrictions reduce household water usage.

items.dataText: DATA: Energy sources used for electricity generation (percentage of total): Country A: Coal 65%, Renewables 18%, Gas 17% Country B: Coal 12%, Renewables 61%, Gas 27% Source: International Energy Agency, 2023.
items.question: Which country relies more on renewable energy, and how much more renewable energy does it use than Country A?

answerKey.reference: Country B relies more on renewable energy (61%) compared to Country A (18%). Country B uses 43 percentage points more renewable energy than Country A.

items.dataText: DATA: Time taken to travel between City P and City Q using different transport: Aeroplane: 1 hour 15 minutes High-speed train: 2 hours 40 minutes Standard train: 4 hours 55 minutes Car: 3 hours 20 minutes (excluding traffic)
items.question: How much faster is the aeroplane than the car for this journey? Use exact figures from the data.

answerKey.reference: The aeroplane takes 1 hour 15 minutes. The car takes 3 hours 20 minutes. The aeroplane is 2 hours 5 minutes faster than the car.

items.dataText: DATA: Percentage of learners who said they felt confident in each subject: Mathematics: 41% English: 67% Science: 53% History: 72% Survey of 500 Grade 5 learners, 2023.
items.question: Which subject has the lowest learner confidence, and how does it compare to the highest?

answerKey.reference: Mathematics has the lowest learner confidence (41%). History has the highest (72%). Learners feel 31 percentage points more confident in History than in Mathematics.

items.dataText: DATA: Average rainfall per year (millimetres): Cape Town: 515 mm Durban: 1 009 mm Johannesburg: 713 mm Upington: 197 mm Source: South African Weather Service.
items.question: Which city receives the most rain, and how does it compare to the driest city listed?

answerKey.reference: Durban receives the most rain (1 009 mm). Upington receives the least (197 mm). Durban gets more than five times as much rain as Upington.

items.dataText: DATA: Favourite sport among 400 learners: Soccer: 180 Netball: 90 Cricket: 70 Athletics: 60 Source: school survey, 2023.
items.question: Which sport is the most popular, and how does it compare to athletics?

answerKey.reference: Soccer is the most popular (180 learners). Athletics is the least popular listed (60 learners). Three times as many learners chose soccer as chose athletics.

items.dataText: DATA: Percentage of waste recycled by material: Glass: 78% Paper: 65% Metal: 52% Plastic: 31% Source: national recycling report.
items.question: Which material is recycled the most, and how does plastic compare?

answerKey.reference: Glass is recycled the most (78%). Plastic is recycled the least (31%). Glass is recycled at more than twice the rate of plastic.

items.dataText: DATA: Average screen time per day (hours): Ages 8–10: 2.5 Ages 11–13: 4.0 Ages 14–16: 6.5 Source: media use study.
items.question: How does screen time change as children get older?

answerKey.reference: Screen time increases with age. The youngest group (ages 8–10) averages 2.5 hours, while the oldest group (ages 14–16) averages 6.5 hours — more than double.

items.dataText: DATA: Number of public libraries per province: Western Cape: 360 Gauteng: 110 KwaZulu-Natal: 215 Free State: 175 Source: provincial library services.
items.question: Which province has the most public libraries, and how does Gauteng compare?

answerKey.reference: The Western Cape has the most public libraries (360). Gauteng has the fewest listed (110). The Western Cape has more than three times as many libraries as Gauteng.

items.dataText: DATA: Litres of water used per activity at home: Bath: 80 Shower (5 min): 45 Washing dishes by hand: 20 Brushing teeth (tap running): 6 Source: water-saving guide.
items.question: Which activity uses the most water, and how does a shower compare to a bath?

answerKey.reference: A bath uses the most water (80 litres). A five-minute shower uses 45 litres, which is almost half as much as a bath, so showering saves water.

items.dataText: DATA: Books borrowed by genre in one month: Adventure: 240 Mystery: 190 Science: 120 Poetry: 50 Source: school library records.

answerKey.reference: Adventure books are borrowed the most (240). Poetry is borrowed the least (50). Almost five times as many adventure books are borrowed as poetry books.

items.title: How Bees Make Honey
items.passage: Bees make honey by collecting nectar from flowers. A worker bee visits hundreds of flowers and sucks up the sweet nectar using its long tongue. The nectar is stored in the bee's honey stomach, where it mixes with enzymes that begin breaking it down into simpler sugars. Back at the hive, the bee passes the nectar to other worker bees, who chew it and continue breaking it down. The bees then spread the nectar into the honeycomb cells, where water evaporates from it over several days. When the honey is thick enough, the bees seal the cell with a wax cap. A single bee produces only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its lifetime.

answerKey.reference: Bees make honey by collecting flower nectar and processing it through a series of steps in the hive. Key details: Bees collect nectar from hundreds of flowers.; Enzymes in the bee's stomach break the nectar down.; Water evaporates from the nectar in the honeycomb before it is sealed.

items.title: Why We Dream
items.passage: Scientists are still not certain why humans dream, but several theories exist. One widely accepted idea is that dreaming helps the brain process and store memories from the day. During a stage of sleep called REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, the brain is very active — almost as active as when we are awake. Some researchers believe that during this time the brain sorts through experiences, strengthening important memories and discarding unneeded information. Another theory suggests that dreaming helps us process emotions, allowing us to work through difficult feelings in a safe environment. A third idea is that dreams are simply a side effect of the brain's normal activity during sleep — meaningful to us but without a specific function.

answerKey.reference: Scientists have several theories about why we dream, most involving memory processing or emotional regulation. Key details: REM sleep is when most dreaming occurs and the brain is very active.; One theory says dreaming helps store memories.; Another theory suggests dreams help us process emotions.

items.title: The History of the Olympic Games
items.passage: The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece around 776 BCE as a religious festival honouring the god Zeus. Athletes from across the Greek world competed in events including running, wrestling, and chariot racing. The Games were held every four years at Olympia and were so important that wars between Greek states were paused to allow athletes to travel safely. The ancient Olympics continued for over 1 000 years before being banned by the Roman Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE. The modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896 in Athens, Greece, largely through the efforts of French educator Pierre de Coubertin. Today the Games are held every four years and involve thousands of athletes from over 200 countries.

answerKey.reference: The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece and were revived in the modern era, becoming the world's largest international sporting event. Key details: The ancient Olympics began around 776 BCE and were held at Olympia.; Wars were paused to allow athletes to travel to the Games.; The modern Olympics were revived in 1896 in Athens.

items.title: The Importance of Sleep
items.passage: Sleep is one of the most important things the human body does, yet many people do not get enough of it. During sleep, the brain consolidates memories, the body repairs damaged tissues, and the immune system is strengthened. Children and teenagers need between 8 and 10 hours of sleep per night, but surveys show that many get far less than this. Lack of sleep affects concentration, mood, and physical performance. Over time, chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to serious health problems including obesity, heart disease, and depression. Sleep experts recommend keeping a consistent sleep schedule, avoiding screens before bed, and ensuring the sleeping environment is dark and cool.

answerKey.reference: Sleep is essential for health and brain function, and most young people do not get enough of it. Key details: During sleep, the brain consolidates memories and the body repairs itself.; Children need 8–10 hours but many get less.; Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to obesity, heart disease, and depression.

items.title: Plastic in the Ocean
items.passage: Plastic pollution in the ocean has become one of the most serious environmental problems of our time. Around 8 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean each year. Much of this plastic does not decompose — instead it breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which are now found in every ocean on Earth, from the surface to the deepest trenches. Marine animals mistake plastic for food, and it has been found in the stomachs of fish, seabirds, and whales. Microplastics have also been detected in human blood and breast milk. Scientists warn that unless plastic production and disposal are significantly reduced, the amount of plastic in the ocean could triple by 2040.

answerKey.reference: Plastic pollution is a major environmental problem, with millions of tonnes entering the ocean each year and harming marine life and humans. Key details: Around 8 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean each year.; Plastic breaks into microplastics that are found throughout the ocean.; Microplastics have been found in marine animals and even in human blood.

items.title: The Development of Language
items.passage: Language is one of the defining features of being human, and it has evolved over hundreds of thousands of years. Scientists believe that early humans began communicating through gestures and simple vocalisations long before spoken language developed. Modern human language — with grammar, complex vocabulary, and the ability to discuss abstract ideas — probably emerged around 100 000 years ago. Children acquire language remarkably quickly: by the age of five, most have mastered the basic grammar of their native language without being explicitly taught it. Today there are approximately 7 000 languages spoken worldwide, though many are endangered as smaller language communities disappear. Linguists estimate that one language dies every two weeks.

answerKey.reference: Human language evolved over thousands of years and children acquire it naturally, but thousands of languages are now endangered. Key details: Modern complex language probably emerged around 100 000 years ago.; Children master basic grammar by age five without being formally taught.; About 7 000 languages exist today, but one dies approximately every two weeks.

items.title: How Earthquakes Are Measured
items.passage: Earthquakes release energy in the form of seismic waves, and scientists use two main scales to measure them. The Richter scale, developed in 1935 by Charles Richter, measures the energy released at the source of the earthquake. Each whole number increase on the scale represents a tenfold increase in the size of the seismic waves. The moment magnitude scale (Mw), developed in the 1970s, is now more widely used by scientists because it is more accurate for large earthquakes. The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale is different — it measures how strongly an earthquake is felt at different locations rather than the energy released. An earthquake measuring 2.0 on the moment magnitude scale is barely noticeable, while one measuring 8.0 or above can destroy entire cities.

answerKey.reference: Scientists use several scales to measure earthquakes, each capturing a different aspect of the earthquake's size or impact. Key details: The Richter scale measures energy at the source; each point represents a tenfold increase.; The moment magnitude scale is now more widely used for large earthquakes.; The MMI scale measures how strongly an earthquake is felt at different locations.

items.title: Food Security
items.passage: Food security means that all people have reliable access to enough nutritious food to live healthy lives. According to the United Nations, approximately 735 million people worldwide are chronically hungry. Food insecurity is caused by a combination of factors including poverty, conflict, climate change, and inefficient food distribution systems. Paradoxically, the world already produces enough food to feed every person on Earth — the problem is that much of it is wasted or unevenly distributed. Around one third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted before it is eaten. Experts argue that solving food insecurity requires not just producing more food, but improving storage, distribution, and reducing waste.

answerKey.reference: Food insecurity affects hundreds of millions of people, but the problem is not a shortage of food — it is waste and unequal distribution. Key details: About 735 million people are chronically hungry worldwide.; The world produces enough food for everyone but much is wasted or unevenly distributed.; Around one third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted.

items.title: Plastic Pollution
items.passage: Plastic pollution is one of the biggest problems facing our oceans today. Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic waste end up in the sea, where it can take hundreds of years to break down. Sea animals such as turtles and seabirds often mistake plastic for food, which can make them very ill or even kill them. Tiny pieces of plastic, called microplastics, have now been found in fish and even in drinking water. Scientists say the best way to solve the problem is to use less plastic, reuse what we can, and recycle the rest.

answerKey.reference: Plastic pollution is harming our oceans and the animals in them, and the best way to fix it is to use less plastic, reuse, and recycle. Key details: Millions of tonnes of plastic enter the sea each year.; Animals mistake plastic for food and become ill.; Tiny microplastics have been found in fish and drinking water.

items.title: The Moon Landing
items.passage: On 20 July 1969, two American astronauts became the first humans to walk on the Moon. Their spacecraft, Apollo 11, had travelled about 384 000 kilometres from Earth. Neil Armstrong was the first to step onto the surface, followed by Buzz Aldrin, while a third astronaut stayed in orbit. They collected rock samples and planted a flag before returning safely to Earth. The Moon landing is remembered as one of the greatest achievements in human history.

answerKey.reference: The first Moon landing in 1969 was a historic achievement in which astronauts walked on the Moon and returned safely. Key details: Apollo 11 travelled about 384 000 kilometres.; Neil Armstrong was the first to step onto the surface.; The astronauts collected rock samples before returning to Earth.

items.title: Antibiotics
items.passage: Antibiotics are powerful medicines that fight infections caused by bacteria. Before they were discovered, even small infections could be deadly. The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, and it has saved millions of lives since. However, doctors warn that using antibiotics too often can make bacteria resistant, which means the medicines stop working. For this reason, antibiotics should only be taken when a doctor says they are needed.

answerKey.reference: Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections and have saved millions of lives, but overusing them can make them stop working. Key details: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.; Before antibiotics, small infections could be deadly.; Overuse makes bacteria resistant to the medicine.

items.title: Migration of the Wildebeest
items.passage: Each year in East Africa, more than a million wildebeest take part in one of nature's greatest journeys. They travel in huge herds across the plains of Tanzania and Kenya in search of fresh grass and water. Along the way they must cross rivers full of crocodiles and avoid predators such as lions. Many animals do not survive the journey, but the migration is essential for the herds to find enough food. The great wildebeest migration draws visitors from all over the world.

answerKey.reference: Over a million wildebeest migrate across East Africa each year to find food and water, facing many dangers along the way. Key details: They travel across Tanzania and Kenya.; They must cross rivers full of crocodiles.; The migration helps the herds find enough grass and water.

items.title: The Importance of Sleep
items.passage: Sleep is just as important for your health as eating well and exercising. While you sleep, your body repairs itself and your brain sorts and stores everything you have learned during the day. Children and teenagers need more sleep than adults because their bodies and brains are still growing. People who do not get enough sleep often find it harder to concentrate, remember things, and control their mood. Experts recommend that young people aim for nine to eleven hours of sleep each night.

answerKey.reference: Sleep is essential for health because it lets the body repair itself and the brain store what you have learned. Key details: Children and teenagers need more sleep than adults.; Too little sleep makes it harder to concentrate and remember.; Experts recommend nine to eleven hours a night for young people.

items.title: The Rainforest Layers
items.passage: A tropical rainforest is made up of several layers, each home to different plants and animals. The top layer is the emergent layer, where the tallest trees rise above the rest. Below it is the canopy, a thick roof of leaves where most rainforest animals live. Further down is the understorey, which is dark and humid, and finally the forest floor, where very little sunlight reaches. Each layer plays an important part in keeping the rainforest alive and balanced.

answerKey.reference: A rainforest has several layers, from the tall emergent layer down to the dark forest floor, and each is home to different living things. Key details: The canopy is where most rainforest animals live.; The understorey is dark and humid.; Very little sunlight reaches the forest floor.

items.title: The Invention of the Telephone
items.passage: The telephone changed the way people communicate forever. Before it was invented, messages had to be sent by letter or telegraph, which could take days. In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell made the first successful telephone call, allowing people to speak to each other over long distances instantly. Over time, telephones became smaller and more common, and today most people carry a mobile phone wherever they go. The telephone is one of the most important inventions in history.

answerKey.reference: The telephone transformed communication by letting people speak instantly over long distances, starting with Bell's first call in 1876. Key details: Before it, messages were sent by letter or telegraph and took days.; Alexander Graham Bell made the first call in 1876.; Telephones became smaller and led to today's mobile phones.
